children: By Staff Writer

Kenya's dominance as East Africa's aviation gateway is under threat as delays in upgrading Jomo Kenyatta International Airport coincide with a regional airport-building race that is rapidly expanding passenger and transit capacity in Ethiopia, Rwanda and Tanzania.

The Kenya Airports Authority says JKIA is operating beyond its intended capacity and risks losing market share to new mega airports such as Ethiopia's Bishoftu Airport and Rwanda's Bugesera International Airport unless expansion plans are fast-tracked.

The Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) is currently handling more passengers than it was designed to and plans to upgrade it are still pending as the State scrambles to obtain financing to move it forward.“There’s a threat of losing market share due to delayed expansion or modernization, especially in light of the rapid development of regional competitors such as Bole lnternational Airport (Addis Ababa), New Kigali lnternational Airport, Bugesera lnternational Airport, Dodoma Msalato lnternational Airport, and Mega Airport City in Bishoftu, Ethiopia,” said the KAA in a recently published disclosure.

With at least 8.9 million passengers travelling though JKIA in 2025, it has been operating far beyond the 7.5 million passengers it was designed to handle every year, exposing passengers to long queues, and degraded facilities such as toilets and waiting bays.

Currently, JKIA is the region’s second busiest airport by passenger traffic, after Addis Ababa’s Bole International Airport which processes roughly 25 million passengers every year, far above the 19 million it was designed to process.
At full completion, the Bishoftu Airport, which will serve as the new hub for Ethiopian Airlines, will serve up to 110 million passengers every year, making it Africa’s largest airport.

The $12.5 billion greenfield project is expected to be fully completed by 2030, capturing more than 10 times JKIA’s capacity and threatening to divert a significant share of international transit traffic from the Nairobi airport.
Competition is also rising from the Bugesera Internaional Airport in Rwanda, whose completion is already ongoing and expected to end by the end of 2028, and begin operations by mid-2029.

When fully completed, it will handle up to 14 million passengers every year, raising Rwanda’s international transit traffic capacity and increasing the current capacity of the Kigali International Airport by up to seven times from the current 2 million.

Modern equipmentTanzania’s Dodoma Msalato Airport also threatens to divert significant traffic from Nairobi. The construction of the airport is almost done, and is set to begin operations soon, becoming the country’s second largest with a capacity of up to 1.75 million passengers per year.

Together with the Julius Nyerere International Airport, which handles up to nine million passengers every year, Msalato airport will eclipse JKIA’s current capacity, risking diversion of some of the traffic.

The upgrade and modernisation of JKIA seeks to improve its capacity from the current 7.5 million to 25 million passengers a year, with the construction of a second terminal with new and modern equipment and facilities.
Although the tender has been awarded to Chinese State-owned contractor China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), construction is yet to begin as the State is yet to raise the required funds.

In a recent interview with The EastAfrican, Kenya’s Roads and Transport Cabinet Secretary Davies Chirchir said the government is in advanced stages of getting a syndicated loan arranged by the Trade and Development Bank (TDB) and the African Finance Corporation (AFC).

The borrowed amount, roughly $630 million, will account for 70 percent of the required $900 million for the airport upgrade, with the remaining 30 percent coming from KAA’s Air Passenger Service Charge (APSC) collections.“We’re basically leveraging the Air Passenger Service Charge tax, to basically sell a portion to raise the 30 percent, and we’ll go the market with a bankable project to raise 70 percent,” said Mr Chirchir.

It recommended that the current terminal be expanded and renovated immediately to boost capacity from the current 7.5 million passengers to 12 million, as construction of the second terminal begins. However, this is yet to happen.

As the hub for the national flag carrier Kenya Airways (KQ), the loss of traffic at JKIA to neighbouring Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Tanzania could be consequential for the airline which is trying to grow its revenues and return to profitability.

All three countries also have their own national airlines, each competing to capture the growing regional air travel market and are banking on improved airport facilities to draw international traffic.

Ethiopian Airlines is currently the region’s largest airline by both fleet size and passenger traffic, after surpassing Kenya Airways over the last decade. KQ is targeting to grow its fleet from the current 45 to 60 by 2030, while expanding its route network, all of which are banked on the improvement of the airport to accommodate increased traffic.
